purpose: Per-subagent model + reasoning-effort routing. Pay peak intelligence once at the orchestrator; farm everything else down the ladder.

benchmark.price: USD per reference task-run, measured locally
benchmark.note: Update prices/index here when tiers change; every rule below is derived from this table.

ladder.note: The rungs agents actually pin. The code side follows the lower-left convex hull of `measured`. The think side deliberately adds two rungs that are NOT hull-optimal per index point (fable-med, opus-xhigh) because they are cheaper in absolute price: a think call that does not need the extra points saves 30-32% on every dispatch, and the ladder never steps more than 1.5x between neighbours.

dominated.reason: opus-low costs $0.01 more (+2%) and scores 9 points higher (+21%). Strictly dominated — never select it.
opus-med costs $0.05 less (-7%) and scores 1 point higher. Strictly dominated — never select it.

off_hull.reason: From opus-med it buys +2 for $0.51 ($0.255/pt). fable-high buys +3 for $0.71 ($0.237/pt) and fable-med buys +1 for $0.28 with a lower absolute price. Squeezed from both sides; this was the pre-1.1 sage tier.

Off the strict hull ($0.28/pt vs fable-high's $0.237/pt from opus-med) but ON the ladder as `critic`: $0.43 cheaper per call than sage, and most judgement calls do not need sage's +2 points. Added in 1.2.0 to close the 2x gap between dev and sage.
On the hull (+1 over fable-high for $0.37) and ON the ladder as `judge` since 1.2.0: $0.85 cheaper per call than oracle. Was the 1.0 oracle tier. Closes the 1.85x gap between sage and oracle.

marginal_cost_per_index_point.interpretation: Climbing to opus-med is cheap. The first step past it is 6.8x more expensive per point and every later step stays in the $0.22-0.43/pt band. Above the cliff choose by absolute price: critic before sage, judge before oracle. fable-max is the worst step on the board ($1.04 for one point) and is never an agent tier.

grunt.label: stupid work
grunt.definition: Retrieval and execution with no judgement call. The answer is already in the repo or in a command's stdout; the agent just has to go get it.
examples: find every file that imports X
run the test suite and report raw failures
list dependency versions / env vars / route definitions
collect and dedupe log lines around a timestamp
check whether a symbol still exists before I recommend it
mechanical exploration where the search pattern is already known

code.label: code
code.definition: Writing or changing code. Split by whether the shape of the change is already decided.

dumb.definition: The change is decided; only typing remains. No invariants at risk.
examples: apply a decided rename/codemod across N files
write tests for behaviour that is already specified
port a known pattern to a new file

smart.definition: The change requires reasoning about correctness while writing it: invariants, concurrency, error paths, non-obvious bugs.
examples: implement a feature end to end
debug a failure whose cause is not yet known
refactor across a boundary that carries invariants
anything touching auth, money, migrations, concurrency, data loss

think.label: think
think.definition: No code produced. Deciding what should happen, or judging whether what happened is right.
examples: verifying one claim before acting on it
synthesizing a handful of subagent reports
design questions the codebase already has a pattern for
hard_only: architecture and design tradeoffs that move a boundary or contract
reviewing a diff that carries auth/money/migration/concurrency invariants
adversarial verification where being wrong is expensive
final synthesis across many subagent reports
peak_only: one-shot but recoverable: a migration with a backup, a release with a rollback, a flag that can be flipped back
a bug that has already defeated dev and sage
the deciding judgement in a workflow whose fan-out cost dwarfs the call
unrecoverable_only: irreversible AND no rollback/backup/flag exists: prod data deletion, key rotation, public security disclosure
ceiling_only: the user asked for max by name
nothing else — $1.04 for one index point is not a routing decision an agent gets to make

escalation.policy: Start at the cheapest plausible tier. Escalate on observed failure, never in anticipation of it.
triggers: the agent returned an empty, hedged, or self-contradictory result
its output failed verification (tests, a check, a reading of the code)
it asked a question it was supposed to answer
same tier has now failed twice on the same task
rules: Do not get expensive unless asked. critic is the autonomous ceiling; sage/judge/oracle require the user to ask in the current message. Two failures at critic = stop and report (what failed, proposed tier, its cost), not escalate.
One rung at a time. Skipping rungs discards the cheap tier's findings.
Pass the failed attempt down as context so the higher tier does not restart from zero.
Two failures at the same rung = escalate, do not retry a third time.
Once the user has granted an escalation, stakes may still skip a rung within the grant (auth/money/migration diff -> sage directly; unrecoverable call -> oracle directly). Difficulty never may.
Never escalate because a task merely sounds important. Escalate because a cheaper attempt actually failed.
There is no rung above oracle. fable-max is reached only when the user names it.

main_loop.rationale: The orchestrator is the think tier and sits on the same rung as sage. Drop to fable medium (critic's rung, -30%) for sessions that are mostly dispatching; xhigh buys +3 index points for +85% and is taken deliberately, not by default.

autonomous_ceiling.rule: Nothing above critic is dispatched on the agent's own judgement. Failure or stakes are reasons to ASK the user for the next rung, naming what failed and what it costs; the user's current message must name the tier or grant the escalation.

workflow_defaults.note: Values for the Workflow tool's agent(prompt, {model, effort, agentType}).
workflow_defaults.shape: Fan out wide and cheap, converge narrow and expensive. Many grunts/chores, critics for the verify fan-out, few sages, at most one judge or oracle per workflow.

rules: Do not get expensive unless asked: sage, judge, oracle and fable-max are user-named tiers. The agent's own ceiling is dev for code and critic for judgement.
Never select sonnet-5: opus-low dominates it on both price and index.
Never select fable-low: opus-med dominates it on both price and index.
Default a subagent to the grunt tier and a judgement to the critic tier; let failure or stakes pull them upward.
opus-med is the ceiling for anything that writes code, unless a cheaper attempt already failed.
critic/sage/judge/oracle do not write code. They decide and they judge.
Above the cliff pick by absolute price: critic before sage ($0.43 less per call), judge before oracle ($0.85 less). The pricier rung is granted by the user, never self-assigned.
fable-max is not a tier. It is a ceiling the user has to ask for by name.
One thinker, many limbs: a single high-tier orchestrator dispatching cheap subagents beats a fleet of expensive ones.
Effort is per-agent and overrides the global effortLevel; a haiku agent under a global xhigh session still runs cheap.
